# Server-Side Chat Moderation

The design — why moderation lives at the homeserver, the two-tier split, and the encryption limit — is owned by the org [trust-and-safety doc](../../../.github/.github/instructions/trust-and-safety.instructions.md); read its **Server-side moderation** section first. This doc records the wiring decisions that doc delegates here. Rollout is tracked in [2-step-choreographer#1746](https://github.com/pangeachat/2-step-choreographer/issues/1746).

Both tiers ship dark: nothing runs until an operator enables a tier in the module's `moderation` config, and Tier 2 refuses to start half-configured — base URL and service token are required at parse time, and the base URL must be a fetchable `http`/`https` URL: ASCII, with a real host, a port in range, no whitespace or control characters, no userinfo marker, and no `?` or `#` anywhere in it. Each of those is a value that used to start cleanly and then fail inside twisted's URI parsing on every message, one swallowed exception at a time. The `?`/`#` rule is not pedantry — `urlparse` reports an empty query and an empty fragment for a trailing one, both falsy, and the endpoint path is appended to the value, so `https://choreo.invalid?` sends every check to `?/choreo/moderate`. `netloc` is not a host test (`https://:443` has one and no host), `@host` is not credential-free just because the userinfo is empty, and `urlparse` raises on a bad port only when `.port` is *read*, which nothing did. The validated, stripped value is what gets stored: validating a copy and keeping the original is how `"https://host "` passed a check it did not satisfy. A non-empty string that is not a URL (`ftp://choreo.invalid`, or a bare hostname) used to start cleanly and then fail on every message inside the fail-open handler, which is indistinguishable from moderation being switched off. A plaintext `http` base URL parses, for local stacks, and logs a WARNING: the service token and every moderated message cross the network in the clear.

**Unknown keys in the `moderation` block are refused at parse time.** Every key in it turns moderation on, so a key silently ignored is a tier silently dark: `tier1_enable: true` (no `d`) parsed cleanly, registered no callback and logged nothing at any level. The error names the key it did not recognise and lists the ones it knows. Configured bot accounts are exempt from both tiers — bot content is governed upstream, and redacting the bot's replies would fight the orchestrator.

## Exempt senders

`moderation.exempt_user_id_globs` lists the senders neither tier ever sees. An exemption is a security boundary, not a convenience filter, so two rules hold.

**Glob syntax, not regular expressions.** `*` matches any run of characters, `?` matches exactly one, and every other character is a literal drawn from the set a Matrix ID is built from (`a-z A-Z 0-9 . _ = / + - @ :`). Anything else — a backslash, a character class, an alternation, an anchor — is refused at parse time. The values only ever describe Matrix IDs, so a regular expression buys nothing, and it is evaluated in the pre-persist send path on every message: a configured pattern such as `@(a+)+:example.org` backtracks catastrophically against a long non-matching Matrix ID and stalls the reactor, where the module's fail-open handling cannot reach it. A consequence worth knowing: a server name written as an IPv6 literal cannot be matched, because `[` and `]` are outside the grammar. Use `*` for the server part.

**The match is whole-string.** `@bot*:example.org` exempts `@bot:example.org` and `@bot-staging:example.org`, and does not exempt `@botimposter:example.org.evil.com`.

A glob of only `*` characters exempts every sender on every homeserver. It parses — that is an operator's call to make — and logs a WARNING naming it.

### Migrating from `exempt_user_id_patterns`

The former key took regular expressions applied with `re.match`, which anchored only the start: `@bot.*:example\.org` exempted `@botimposter:example.org.evil.com` from both tiers. Startup now **refuses** the old key outright — its presence is what is refused, so an empty list or a bare `exempt_user_id_patterns:` is refused too — and names each configured value with a suggested glob. Nothing is translated automatically, because the two grammars overlap and disagree — `@bot?:example.org` is valid in both, and means `@bot:example.org` as a regex and `@bota:example.org` as a glob — so an automatic conversion could silently widen an exemption. Restate each value and check it says what you meant.

## Tier 1 — deterministic pre-filter (blocks on send)

Runs in the send path and can reject a message before it appears, so everything here must stay model-free and sub-millisecond. A wrongly blocked ordinary message is worse than a miss (Tier 2 and human reporting back this up), so every pattern leans conservative:

- **Phone numbers** — the `phonenumbers` library (libphonenumber port), matching valid numbers only. Bare national formats match for the configured regions; international `+CC` formats match regardless. A bare year or house count does not trip it. `moderation.tier1_phone_regions` is checked against libphonenumber's own region list at parse time and must name at least one region: the matcher loops over the regions it is given, so `[]`, `"us"` and `"US "` are all lists of strings that make the phone rule find nothing and say nothing. Use uppercase ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 codes. There is no way to ask for international formats only — libphonenumber still needs a region to match against.
- **Profanity** — the **universal core** of the wordlist: the terms with no benign homograph in any supported language. Everything ambiguous is Tier 2's. The core is matched losslessly and by whole token — casefold, drop invisible characters, NFC, collapse runs of three or more identical characters, and nothing else. Every further fold is a way for an ordinary word to become a needle: stripping diacritics merged Slovak *pica* with Czech *píča* and Hindi *रोड* (road) with *रंडी* (a slur), and prefix matching blocked Romanian *curva* on the needle *cu* and the token *хуйский* on *хуй*. Inflections are carried as their own wordlist entries instead of being reached by prefix. An English-only wordlist was the first implementation and was blind in 23 of our 24 full-support languages; a union of all 30 matched by prefix through a lossy normalizer was the next, and it blocked *Merg cu tine*, *रोड पर ट्रैफिक है* and *Pedestrian crossing is ahead*.
- **A term reaches Tier 1 only on POSITIVE evidence, recorded per term.** `moderation/tier1_universal.json` carries one decision for each of the 500 wordlist terms. A `tier1: true` entry must name the basis: `not_a_word_or_an_identifier` (below), `curator_attested` (English, checked by a native English speaker, and the three words are listed in the policy block), or `native_review` (a named native speaker and date). **There are no native reviews, so 29 languages have no plain-word terms in Tier 1 at all.** Adding one is a review task, not a code change.

- **A digit inside a needle is not evidence on its own.** The basis used to read "the needle contains a digit, so it can only match a deliberately obfuscated spelling". The first half is true and the second does not follow: ALPHANUMERIC IDENTIFIERS — gamertags, room and apartment codes, SKUs, model numbers, usernames — substitute a digit for a letter as a matter of course and are ordinary chat content. `check_text("Room P1CA is down the hall")` and `check_text("Model P1CA-200 ships Friday")` were both `M_FORBIDDEN`. What the digit does is narrow the question from "is this a word in one of thirty languages?", which nobody here can answer, to "does an ordinary identifier get spelled this way?", which the recorded readings can: **a leet form inherits the readings of the word it spells.** `P1CA` reads as a stylized `Pica` — a typographic unit, and an ordinary word in Catalan, Portuguese and Spanish — while `4RSCHLOCH` spells nothing but the slur. So a needle with a de-leeting in `skeletons_with_a_benign_reading`, or one matching a term the file demotes for a recorded benign reading, stays Tier 2 with reason `identifier_reading`. Five did: `p 1 c a`, `g3ci`, `p0ndan`, `v1ado`, `p3der`. The gate re-derives this per term from both sources rather than reading a sentence written beside it, so deleting the policy entry does not re-promote a term the wordlist already demotes. The irony is recorded so it is not repeated: `pica` was demoted for exactly this ambiguity, and its leetspeak form carried the identical collision back in.

- **A term written with its letters separated may only match a spelled-out run.** `needle()` strips every separator — it has to, because `f*ck` and `k.u.r.v.a` are one word with its letters split — so `p 1 c a`, authored as a spaced spelling, was stored as the compact needle `p1ca` and went into the bucket that matches any whole token. `match_bucket` now splits the three: `token` (compact), `phrase` (a run of whole words), and `split` (spaced letters only). The rejoining scan sees `token ∪ split`, so moving a needle out of `token` does not stop it catching what it was written for; whole-token equality sees `token` alone. Nothing is in `split` today, and the rule is gated on the classifier and on synthetic records rather than on live data for that reason — an assertion over an empty set protects nothing, which is how this survived in the first place.
- **Absence of a collision is not evidence, and that was learned the expensive way.** The first version of this promoted any term the frequency gate did not object to - 414 of 500. Three rounds of adversarial review then found, among terms scoring zero in every language the gate could measure: *faggot* (a British dish, Oxford Learner's Dictionary), *hoer* (one who hoes, Merriam-Webster), Greek *καριόλα* (a bed), Turkish *kaltak* (a saddle frame), Portuguese *viado* (striped fabric), Korean *병신* (the sexagenary year 丙申), Indonesian *pondan* (a baking-mix brand) and *Chuj* (a Mayan language). The rate of discovery was not falling. A rule that admits a term because nothing objected admits every one of those.
- **`wordfreq` is the tripwire on top, never the decider.** For every term, the gate records the languages where the surface form is measurable and requires a written adjudication of `no_benign_sense` for each. Frequency measures how often a form is written, not whether it is benign - `fuck` scores 4.85 in Danish and 4.29 in German as a borrowed swear - so a high score forces adjudication and a low score approves nothing (`zipf_frequency('pica', 'sk')` is 0.0). `tests/test_moderation_tier1_terms.py` re-measures every recorded number.
- **Tier 1 never matches inside a word, and never across a sentence.** Whole tokens, or a run of whole words of one sentence. There is no substring matching, which is why **Chinese and Japanese have no Tier 1 coverage at all**: a script written without word spacing gives a needle no boundary to respect, and `操你妈` is spread across 体操 / 你 / 妈妈 in "can your mother do this gymnastics routine". Deciding where a Chinese word ends needs segmentation, which is Tier 2's to do. A phrase that could form across a full stop is the same defect one level up: `chữ pê. Đê là` is two Vietnamese letter names.
- **Rejoining split letters is restricted by script.** `f*ck` and `f u c k` rejoin because punctuation is never a word boundary and one Latin character is one letter. One Hangul syllable is a whole word - `민수 씨 발 아파요?` is "Minsu, does your foot hurt?" - so nothing rejoins across a space unless every fragment is a single character of an alphabet. Spaced-out evasions in Hangul, kana and the abugidas are Tier 2's.
- **No language identification, anywhere in Tier 1.** Neither `check_text` nor `matches_tier1` takes a language, so no caller can select behaviour by guessing one. LID is unreliable at chat length and structurally broken on code-switched text, and a wrong guess could only ever make Tier 1 block something it should not.

**A failure inside Tier 1 allows the message, and it does so for the WHOLE tier.** If any rule cannot complete, the tier has no verdict and the message goes through (logged, and Tier 2 still sees it). The predecessor caught the phone matcher's exception inside `contains_phone_number` and returned `False`, which is not "no phone number here" but "we do not know" wearing the answer's clothes: the next rule then ran and the message was rejected on its verdict, on the strength of a Tier 1 run that had already failed. A partial failure is never laundered into a clean negative — `check_text` runs the rules from one table and raises `Tier1RuleError` on any of them, so a rule added later inherits the policy without anybody remembering to give it one.

Each check has a rule identifier, which is what appears in logs:

| Rule identifier | The check that fired |
|---|---|
| `contact_details` | phone numbers |
| `profanity` | the wordlist |


### What Tier 1 deliberately does not block

**Street addresses are not a Tier 1 rule.** A pattern cannot tell a shared address from a discussed one, and in a language-learning room the innocent readings dominate: landmarks are a stock topic and naming where you live is an A1 lesson. Tier 1 rejects before persist, so an address pattern here silenced learners writing "10 Downing Street is where the Prime Minister lives" and "I live at 42 Maple Street". Judging an address needs context Tier 1 does not have, so it belongs to Tier 2. Note what this costs until Tier 2 can do it: the provider's category list is an abuse taxonomy (harassment, hate, illicit, self-harm, sexual, violence) with no contact-details category, so **no tier detects address sharing today**.

Because Tier 1 blocks before a message is sent, a false positive silences an innocent learner, which is worse than a miss that Tier 2 can still catch. Terms whose ordinary meaning is common therefore stay out of the blocking core and are left to Tier 2's contextual judgement — animal words used as insults (Malay *babi*, Danish *svin*), body or object words (Polish *pedał*, a bicycle pedal), place and people names (the country Niger, Italian *Troia*), scientific vocabulary (*Homo* sapiens), medical terms (Dutch *kanker*), and every term a supported language uses benignly (Romanian *cu*, Indonesian *kurva* for a curve, Serbian *puta* for "times", Slovak *pica*). The reason for each is recorded per term in `tier1_universal.json`; the corpus's `curation_decisions` records what was dropped from the wordlist outright.

**A rejoined run blocks pre-send only when it carries a DIGIT.** `Press C,U,N,T to continue.` was `M_FORBIDDEN` while `Press C, U, N, T to continue.` passed — the same sentence typed two ways — and every separator-based rule that replaced it produced another ordinary sentence: `The letters are C U N T.` is a spelling lesson with no punctuation at all, `The symbols are Cu,N,T.` is a chemistry lesson, and `Open cu.nt in your editor.` is a filename. Spelling a word out is a first-week classroom exercise and is structurally identical to spelling one out to evade a filter.

A rejoined RUN carrying a digit is a different case from a compact token carrying one, and only the run is unambiguous: a run is spaced letters, which no identifier is. That is the same evidence standard the promotion policy applies to a term (`not_a_word_or_an_identifier`), applied to the rejoining — and the rejoining is the half that held, because the compact half is where an identifier lives. Only across WHITESPACE ALONE, and not across a LINE BREAK — a newline is a stronger boundary than a space, and the rendered text of a table row, a list or a `<br>` is full of them, so `<ol><li>v</li><li>1</li><li>t</li><li>t</li><li>u</li></ol>` was `M_FORBIDDEN`. Punctuation between two pieces is how an identifier is written, not how a word is broken, and rejoining across it blocked `Download the cert from p3.der and install it.` (the standard DER certificate extension), `The API path is /api/v1/ado for now.` and `Our domain is p1.ca and it works.` — 198 blocking forms across `.`, `-` and `/`. `v 1 t t u` and `n 1 g g e r` still block; `c u n t`, `f.u.c.k`, `cu.nt` and `n1.gger` are Tier 2's, with the corpus recording the move. (`p 1 c a` was the exemplar here until the term itself left Tier 1 — see the identifier rule above.) The scan is bounded by the longest needle and never rebuilds its run: before that it was quadratic, and a 60 KB message of spaced single characters took **4.6 seconds** inline in the send path, on a single-threaded reactor.

**A known benign reading demotes the term, whatever kind of word it is.** `tier1_universal.json` previously exempted proper nouns and case-sensitive technical identifiers from demotion and recorded them on the term as accepted pre-send false positives. That contradicted the decision rule stated in the same file, and both entries were reproducible blocks of ordinary sentences: `The fucK gene encodes L-fuculokinase.` (`fucK` is the gene symbol for L-fuculokinase, NCBI gene 946022, and Tier 1 casefolds) and `The Austrian village of Fucking was renamed Fugging in 2021.` The exemption and the key that carried it are gone, `fuck` and `fucking` are Tier 2's, and a test fails on any entry that brings the key back.

**The *pica* collision is resolved, not accepted.** Tier 1 no longer strips diacritics, so *pica* and *píča* are two different tokens, and bare *pica* is Tier 2 only because Catalan, Portuguese and Spanish all use it. The sentence that was previously blocked is a permanent negative control.

**A negative control is never retired because the matcher fails it.** Eight were, and seven of the eight were failures the code should have been fixed for; they are live again, and `TestRestoredControlsCannotBeRetiredAgain` iterates the record of the restoration, so deleting the record fails the suite too.

**The wordlist has not been reviewed by native speakers.** It was LLM-generated and curated by one non-native curator, and the frequency gate sees only what a frequency list can see — it is blind to register, regional sense, reclaimed usage, and to every language `wordfreq` does not carry. `no_collision_measured` means nothing objected, not that a term is verified safe. Four terms left Tier 1 on exactly that point, each one scoring zero everywhere the gate could look: *faggot* is also a British dish in the Oxford Learner's Dictionary, *hoer* is one who hoes in Merriam-Webster, Korean *병신* is also the sexagenary year 丙申, and *pondan* is an Indonesian baking-mix brand.

## Tier 2 — LLM moderation (redacts after)

Fires after an event persists, from a background task so event persistence never waits on HTTP. It calls the choreographer's shared moderation handler (the org doc's single engine rule) authenticated as a dedicated moderation service account — the endpoint accepts any valid token on this homeserver. Category names are normalized onto the orchestrator's flag vocabulary so both moderation paths speak one language.

Category names are checked against the provider's documented vocabulary before they are used. A category is a free-form string from a service we do not run, and it ends up in a log line and in the redaction reason that lands in the room, so anything outside the documented list — including anything that is not a string — becomes the constant `other` and the value the service sent is discarded. A response of `{"flagged": true, "categories": ["@alice:example.org"]}` otherwise published that Matrix ID to the room and to the logs by a route no review of our own format strings would find. The client validates the response's shape at the same boundary: `flagged` must be a bool and `categories` a list of strings, or there is no verdict.

**Self-harm is preserved, not redacted, and the decision is durable.** A learner disclosing that they intend to harm themselves is asking for help, and the message is the only record that they did. Every category in the verdict is examined rather than the one summarised for the log line, so a verdict carrying both harassment and self-harm preserves.

"Never redacted" is a guarantee only if it survives everything a process can lose, and on in-memory state it did not: preserving recorded no decision anywhere, so the same event delivered twice — `self-harm/intent` first, `harassment` second — was redacted by the second verdict, and a restart or a second instance lost the protection for the same reason. The decision is therefore a row in `pangea_moderation_disposition` (event id, room id, disposition, category, timestamp, claim id — never the sender's Matrix ID and never a word of the message), created on first use like `pangea_delete_user_schedule`.

Redaction takes the row as an **atomic claim**: `INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` followed by a read of the row in the same transaction, so exactly one of `preserved` and `redacted` lands and the loser is told which won. A read-then-redact would still have a window where two verdicts both see an empty table. The claim is released when no redaction was sent, so a transient send failure does not make a message permanently un-redactable — and, as a side effect, two instances now send one redaction for a message rather than two.

The preserve and the claim are deliberately asymmetric. A claim is PROVISIONAL — it is released when the send does not happen — so a preserve that arrived while one was outstanding and did nothing would vanish with the release, and the next verdict would redact the disclosure; the preserve therefore takes the row from an outstanding claim, and nothing takes a `preserved` row back. A release is scoped to its own claim id, so it can remove neither a preserve that displaced it nor another instance's claim. A preserve the database refused is retried, and retried *before* any claim is granted, so a database that was briefly unavailable cannot leave a disclosure unprotected once it comes back — in that process. The retry queue is in memory, so a restart before it lands loses the decision and a later verdict will redact; there is no closing that from here, because the only durable place to record "we could not record this" is the store that just refused. It is counted and logged at ERROR, and while the store is refusing it is also refusing every claim, so nothing is being redacted meanwhile. The other side of the same rule: a preserve that can never be written wedges every redaction in that process, which is the safe direction and a whole-feature outage from one row. The claim is taken after the pre-send re-read, with no `await` before the send, and settled through a detached call so a cancellation cannot strand it.

**A claim is given back only when the send provably did NOT happen.** Release used to be the default on every exit from the handler, and that is the wrong shape, because cancellation does not roll back statements that already completed: the durable write is inside Synapse's `handle_new_client_event`, and the fan-out to pushers, the notifier and the third-party rules runs after it, so `worker.cancel()` at the drain deadline can deliver `CancelledError` into a coroutine whose redaction is already in the room. Releasing then erased the only record that a redaction had been taken, counted a landed send as a failure, and skipped the redacted-after-preserve report — for a message nobody can get back. So a raise from the send is an UNKNOWN, resolved by re-reading the event: redacted → keep the claim, count a redaction, and run the same report the success path runs; present and not redacted → the send did not happen, count the failure and release; unreadable or gone → keep the claim, counted under `pangea_moderation_tier2_claim_retained_total{evidence="unknown"}`. A kept claim blocks later verdicts on one event and a human can clear the row; a released one on a message that is already gone leaves a safeguarding table that has forgotten the redaction. The re-read is a second reader of the row the pre-send guard reads and deliberately not the same function — the two want opposite things from an unknown (skip the redaction / keep the claim), and one `except` cannot serve two contradictory defaults.

Placeholders are `?`. `Sqlite3Engine.convert_param_style` returns the SQL unchanged and only `PostgresEngine` rewrites (`?` → `%s`), so `%s` is Postgres-only — and an end-to-end test that boots Postgres alone cannot see that a SQLite deployment would record no decisions at all. The same correction applies to `pangea_delete_user_schedule`, which had it too.

**A flagged verdict we cannot read is never a redaction either.** `categories: null` is a present key with an unusable value, and reading it as absent made a flagged verdict with no category — which redacts, including when the category the service meant to send was self-harm. A flagged verdict without a non-empty list of category strings is preserved. So is one whose category is self-harm-shaped but outside our pinned vocabulary: an unrecognised name normalises to `other`, and `other` redacts, so `self-harm/invented-next-year` would have deleted a disclosure. `evaluated` must be a bool, because the caller tests `is False` and `0` or `"false"` read as a successful evaluation.

**The limit the table cannot close, stated exactly.** A redaction is an irreversible action taken in another system, so the guarantee is about the order of DECISIONS: once an event is recorded preserved, no later decision may redact it. A preserve arriving *after* the redaction decision was taken — in the window between the claim committing and the send landing — cannot recall it. Inside one instance that window is unreachable, because the dispatcher holds one in-flight claim per event id and there is never a second verdict for the same event at the same time; it is reachable only when two instances both run background tasks, which is the misconfiguration `should_run_background_tasks` exists to prevent and which `pangea_moderation_tier2_active` makes visible — `sum(...) > 1` is the alert. When it does happen the redaction is counted under `pangea_moderation_tier2_redacted_after_preserve_total` and logged at ERROR with the room and the event, because a disclosure has been removed and the only remaining remedy is a human who knows that it was.

**A disposition we cannot read is never a redaction.** This is the one decision in the module that does not fail towards carrying on: a message left standing can still be taken down by a human, a deleted disclosure cannot be brought back, and the person it belonged to is the person least able to absorb the mistake. The skip is counted (`redaction_skipped{cause=disposition_unknown}`), as is a preserve that could not be written.

Preserving is still the whole of the response today and is not sufficient on its own: nothing routes the finding to a teacher or safeguarding contact, so a preserved flag reaches the logs and stops there. That path is [pangeachat/admin-dash#105](https://github.com/pangeachat/admin-dash/issues/105).

**Every other flagged category is redacted, and the disposition is self-redaction: the redaction is sent as the offending sender.** The module send path enforces normal room power levels, and no service user is a member of every room — but a sender may always redact their own message, so self-redaction works in every room, DMs included. The moderation reason rides on the redaction event, prefixed so clients and audits can tell moderation redactions from ordinary ones. (This corrects the org doc's assumption that the module send path is privileged; it is not.)

The transport reads the response body itself rather than through `twisted.web.client.readBody`, and the reason is the same in both halves: `readBody` has no size cap, so a peer that streams forever fills the process's memory, and its cancellation path calls `transport.abortConnection()` only *if* the transport has one — which the `TransportProxyProducer` an `Agent` response delivers does not. Cancelling it therefore fires the deferred and leaves the socket open with the body still arriving: the check "times out" while the peer keeps sending. The replacement caps the body at 1 MiB and tears the connection down — `abortConnection` on the real transport underneath when it can be reached, `stopProducing`/`loseConnection` otherwise. **Teardown of the whole exchange is still not guaranteed**, and that is stated rather than implied: `loseConnection` waits for buffered writes and registered producers, so a peer that stops reading our request body can hold the connection after the verdict has been returned and the deadline cancelled. What the deadline guarantees is that the *check* completes and that no unbounded amount of memory is consumed; the socket's lifetime is twisted's, and it is another reason the move to `ModuleApi.http_client` is worth making. The 15-second budget covers the whole exchange — connect, headers and body — because `agent.request`'s own deferred fires as soon as the response HEADERS arrive, so its timeout is already spent by the time the body read starts.

**Tier 2 does not run through an HTTP proxy, and refuses to start if one is in the way.** Synapse's proxy CONNECT waits on a Deferred with no canceller and no transport behind it, so a proxy that accepts TCP and never answers CONNECT survives every deadline this module has: `request.cancel()` ends our wait and closes nothing, and the breaker's half-open probe opens another socket every cooldown for as long as the process runs. The bounded queue, the worker pool and the deadlines do not prevent file-descriptor exhaustion, which takes the homeserver down rather than moderation alone. Closing it inside the transport means re-implementing Synapse's proxy client with its TLS verification and IP policy; capping the attempts bounds the descriptors and wedges Tier 2 permanently once the cap fills. So the module asks the agent whether a proxy stands in front of `choreo_base_url`, honours `no_proxy` through Synapse's own helper, and raises at startup if one does — naming the two fixes, an exemption for the moderation host or `tier2_enabled: false`. A proxy configuration it cannot read refuses too.

**The deterministic wordlist runs beside the service verdict, and only counts.** `profanity.contains_profanity` — the ~470-term multilingual matcher — had no production caller at all, which made Tier 2 LLM-only. It now runs on every Tier-2 message and publishes an agreement matrix, `pangea_moderation_tier2_matcher_agreement_total{service,matcher}` over `flagged|clean|no_verdict` and `hit|miss|error`. It does **not** redact: the list is noisy, notably in Korean where an ordinary bound noun meaning "year" is on it as a slur, so promoting it to a second redaction trigger unmeasured would delete innocent learners' messages in the languages nobody here can read. The matrix makes the service's real miss rate measurable on staging, after which promotion is a decision taken on evidence. Both sides read the same 10,000-character prefix the endpoint reads, or the disagreements would be an artifact of the endpoint's truncation. The matcher's rejoining scan abandons a window as soon as it can no longer become a needle; without that, a 10,000-character message of short tokens cost about 88 ms of reactor time per message.

Tier 2 skips rooms carrying an activity-plan state event: the conversation orchestrator already moderates activity sessions, and a second check would double-redact and double-spend. Every failure in the check-and-redact path is logged and fails open, mirroring the choreo handler's own contract.

**A shutdown that has returned cannot change a room.** The drain writes off whatever is still in flight at its deadline, and writing off the accounting is not the same as stopping the work: an abandoned job used to wake up afterwards, read the database and send a redaction. Abandoned workers are cancelled, and — because `CancelledError` is an `Exception` and every handler here catches those by design — the dispatcher also refuses work once the drain has **ended**, which the redaction path checks before it sends. The refusal is on the end of the drain rather than its start, so a job that finishes inside the window still redacts. A preserved disposition is still recorded on the way down: writing that down can only keep a message up.

### What both tiers read from an event

**The rule: what the rules see is never less than what a reader sees.** An extractor that returns a subset of the displayed text is not a missed detection — it is a bypass any sender can trigger on every message — so where the displayed text is ambiguous, the union of the candidate surfaces is moderated. Over-reading costs a false positive on one message; under-reading costs the tier.

In practice:

- The outer `body` and `formatted_body` are always read. An edit **adds** `m.new_content`'s surfaces rather than replacing them (ADR-8a(0)): modern clients render `m.new_content`, older clients render the outer `* <new text>` fallback, so choosing one leaves the other unmoderated in whichever client renders it.
- `m.new_content` is read **only** when the event's own `m.relates_to.rel_type` is `m.replace`. Preferring it on presence alone was a total bypass of both tiers — `{"msgtype": "m.text", "body": "<payload>", "m.new_content": {}}` is displayed as the payload by every client and extracted as nothing at all. Tier 1 trusts the event's own `rel_type` and does not verify the relation; establishing that the target exists, is in the same room and has the same sender needs a database read the send path cannot afford, so a bogus relation makes Tier 1 read a field no client displays. That direction is a known false positive, and the validated attribution lands with the Tier-2 disposition work.
- Content is read as any `Mapping`, not as `dict`: Synapse's Rust event type and a homeserver running `use_frozen_dicts: true` both hand modules content that is not a plain dict, and a `dict` test on either would silently stop moderating every edit.
- **There is no msgtype allowlist.** `body` is, by the spec's own definition, "a textual representation of the message", and clients render it for every msgtype — as an image's caption, as a location's description, and as the whole message for a msgtype they do not recognise. An allowlist of `m.text`/`m.image`/… therefore handed any sender a one-field bypass: `{"msgtype": "m.not-a-real-type", "body": "<payload>"}` is displayed as the payload and matched an allowlist of nothing. The event TYPE is the gate; inside `m.room.message`, every displayed string is read.
- A `body` that is not a string is stringified rather than dropped. Synapse's `EventValidator` runs on events this homeserver *creates* and does require a string `body`; `on_new_event` also sees events that arrived over federation, where the sending homeserver decides what passes, and a client that renders a non-string field renders `str(...)` of it. Malformed is not the same as absent.
- An attachment's `filename` is read as well as its `body`: clients show the original filename beside the caption whenever the two differ, so it is displayed text.
- `formatted_body` is reduced to displayed text by a real HTML parser, not a regex. Tags are stripped before entities are decoded, so `&lt;I will kill you&gt;` becomes the visible text `<I will kill you>` rather than being decoded into a tag and deleted. Inline elements concatenate (`4<b>1</b>5` is one number on screen) and block elements break the line. A `<` that is not followed by an ASCII letter is a character, not a tag opener, which is what HTML5 says and what the regex got wrong: it deleted `<415-555-2671 >` outright.
- **Two places where Python's `HTMLParser` disagrees with HTML5, both of which hid a whole message.** `<!-->` closes the comment immediately under HTML5 and everything after it is on screen; Python reads it as an *open* comment and scans for a later terminator, swallowing the lot, so `<!-->call 415-555-2671<!-- -->` was a phone number to every reader and nothing at all to the extractor. And HTML5 has no CDATA in an HTML body — `<![CDATA[` opens a bogus comment that ends at the first `>` — while Python swallows the whole section up to `]]>`. Both are normalised back to what a renderer shows.
- A NUL becomes U+FFFD, which is what HTML5 does with it — deleting it joined digits either side into a number nobody sees, and inside a tag name it turned an unknown element into a real `script` and hid the element's contents.
- There is **no doctype preprocessing**, deliberately. A `>` inside a quoted public or system identifier does end the doctype under HTML5, which is what Python's parser already does; a quote-aware scan added to "fix" that deleted displayed text, mangled doctype-shaped text inside an `alt` value, and recursed once per declaration.
- **Attribute text is read for the tag/attribute pairs a renderer actually displays**, and collected into a second stream appended at the end rather than spliced in where the tag stood. Both halves matter: `alt` on an `<img>` is shown when the image does not load and `alt` on a `<b>` is shown by nothing, so matching on the attribute *name* made `<b alt="415-555-2671">hello</b>` a Tier-1 block on a message reading "hello"; and splicing the value inline broke `41<b title="notes">5</b>-555-2671`, which reads `415-555-2671` on screen, in half. The pairs are `img alt`, `img title`, `a title`, `abbr title`, `span data-mx-spoiler`, `span data-mx-maths` and `div data-mx-maths`.
- `<script>` and `<style>` content is **not** read. Nobody reads a stylesheet, so matching one is a false positive with no upside.
- An unterminated tag at the end of the string is **not** read. HTML5 ends the tokenizer inside the tag state at end-of-input and emits nothing, so no renderer shows it; an earlier revision appended its raw tail on the theory that over-reading is always the safe error, and it is not — Tier 1 blocks before persist.

- **Text inside a table but outside a cell is displayed BEFORE the table.** HTML5 calls it foster parenting, and every browser does it: `<table>41<tr><td>notes</td></tr>5-555-2671</table>` reads as `415-555-2671` followed by a one-cell table, while this extractor reads source order. **It reports that rather than repairing it.** Three attempts to synthesise the reader's order were each wrong in a new place — a missed number when a row held the text, a missed number when one `<div>` sat inside a cell, and an *invented* number across a nested table, which is a pre-send block on text nobody sees. Getting it right needs the insertion modes and the element stack of a real tree builder, which is out of scope here. So the case is made safe instead: the extraction is marked incomplete, which counts it and hands the message to Tier 2, and the tier that blocks does not act on a reading we know is not the reader's.

**A failure to READ is not a finding of NOTHING.** A `formatted_body` that broke the parser used to take the whole event with it, including the plain `body` that had already been read: ~4 KB of nested CDATA sections raised `RecursionError`, both tiers saw a message with no text, and the dropped counter moved by zero — a bypass any sender could trigger on every message, invisible on every dashboard. Every surface, and every field within a surface, is now read inside its own guard; the shortfall is counted as `pangea_moderation_extraction_incomplete_total` per tier, and Tier 2 still receives whatever was read. When nothing at all could be read it is a counted drop (`extraction_failed`), never a message that passed. `on_new_event`'s own fail-open handler counts too (`dispatch_error`). This is the rule `tier1_prefilter.check_text` already states for the RULES — a partial failure must not become a clean negative — applied one layer up, in the extraction that feeds them.

The recursion itself is gone at the mechanism rather than caught: `<![` is rewritten so Python's parser reaches its own bogus-comment branch, which is the reading HTML5 specifies, in one flat parse however deep the nesting — and it also fixes an unterminated section, which used to swallow the rest of the message.

Two limits, stated rather than claimed away: `href` is **not** read (clients display the link's text, and a URL full of digits is a plausible phone-rule false positive), and text a client renders only after running a sanitiser we do not run may differ from what this extractor sees.

## What a moderation log line may contain

A moderation log record is not an ordinary diagnostic: it states that a particular person tripped a content filter, and it says something about what they wrote. Application logs are not an access-controlled store, they are shipped to aggregators, and they outlive the decision by months. So the module holds to one rule: **no Matrix ID and no message text ever reaches a log handler.**

What a line does carry is a room id, an event id where one exists, the rule identifier from the table above, and a `sender_digest`. The digest is a keyed hash of the Matrix ID with a key generated once per process: an operator chasing a false positive can see that the same sender tripped a rule repeatedly, and the value cannot be turned back into a Matrix ID — not even by enumerating the homeserver's users, which a plain hash would allow. Correlation stops at the process boundary on purpose; anything longer-lived is a behavioural record of a named person and belongs in the database, behind authorisation. An event id resolves to its sender the same way.

A redaction that cannot be sent is caught inside `_check_and_redact` rather than allowed to propagate. It runs under `run_as_background_process`, which logs whatever reaches it — and Synapse's own "User &lt;mxid&gt; not in room &lt;room&gt;" carries the Matrix ID, which is the ordinary case in a DM the offender leaves. Counting those failures and escalating the legitimate ones is separate work; today the message stays up and the failure is visible.

Exceptions are the channel that is easy to miss. `logger.exception` prints the exception's own message, and a library that fails on a message body routinely quotes that body back, so no moderation handler logs a traceback. Each logs the exception's type and the `file:line` that raised it, which is what identifies a bug, and nothing that came from the message.

Rule identifiers name the **rule**, not the category of personal data it looks for, for the same reason: `rule=phone_number` beside a room id is an assertion about what a specific message contained.

### The identity Synapse attaches, and how it is removed

`synapse.config.logger.one_time_logging_setup` does not attach `LoggingContextFilter` to a logger or a handler — it replaces the process's **log-record factory**, so every record created anywhere in the process is decorated at creation with the in-flight request's `requester` and `authenticated_entity`: the sender's Matrix ID, on every moderation record, whatever the format string says. The shipped `precise` formatter prints neither, which is exactly why this survives review; a structured-logging sink serialises the whole record.

The module removes them. `log_safety.scrubbing_logger` attaches a filter to each of the package's loggers, and the placement is the point: `Logger.handle` runs the logger's own filters **before** `callHandlers` walks the ancestor chain, so one filter covers every handler the record could reach, root handlers and structured sinks included. `requester`, `authenticated_entity`, `ip_address` and `user_agent` are replaced with a constant rather than deleted, so a deployment whose formatter names `%(requester)s` still formats. `url` is dropped whole. `server_name`, `site_tag`, `method` and `protocol` are left alone — they name an endpoint and a request, not a person. `request` (the request id) is kept only in the shape Synapse generates, `METHOD-sequence`: `get_request_id` returns the value of the `request_id_header` verbatim when a deployment configures one, so a client sending `X-Request-ID: @alice:example.org` otherwise puts its own Matrix ID on every record of its own request — and the shipped `precise` formatter prints this field, so that leaks with no structured logging at all.

`url` is redacted whole rather than cleaned. The first attempt kept the path and scrubbed Matrix-ID-shaped substrings out of it, which does not work: a Matrix URL carries client-chosen text in several places at once — a transaction id is whatever the client typed, `%40alice%3Aexample.org` is a Matrix ID no pattern over the decoded form will find, and a localpart may contain a `/`. `get_redacted_uri` removes access tokens and client secrets, not arbitrary request data. `method` and the request id stay, and Synapse's own request lines carry the URL for an operator who needs it.

**Every logger in `synapse_pangea_chat/moderation/` must be obtained from `scrubbing_logger`, not from `logging.getLogger`.** A logger's filters apply only to records logged through that logger — `callHandlers` inherits an ancestor's handlers, never its filters — so a new file with a bare `getLogger` reopens the channel for its own records. `tests/test_moderation_logging.py::ModerationLoggerCoverageTestCase` walks the package and fails if one is missed.

**A second copy of the filter goes on the handlers**, once, when moderation starts — on the package logger's handlers, its ancestors', its *descendants'*, and on whatever a handler forwards to (a `MemoryHandler` re-runs its target's filters, and Synapse's shipped logging configuration uses exactly that buffer-to-target shape). The last is not redundant: walking upwards covers the handlers a record propagates to, and a handler attached directly to `moderation.tier1_prefilter` is not on that path while being the first thing a record from that logger reaches. Synapse still supports attaching `LoggingContextFilter` to a *handler*, and `Handler.handle` runs its own filters after the logger's — so such a handler re-derives the identity from the logcontext and puts it back on a record we had already cleaned. The handler copy is scoped to this package's records: stripping the requester from Synapse's own request log is not ours to do, and it is the identity an operator relies on everywhere else. Residue: a handler attached *after* moderation starts, by a logging-configuration reload, is not covered.

### What this rule still does not reach

The rule governs records this module creates. One channel sits outside it, and it is a property of Synapse rather than of this module:

- **Synapse's own records, on Synapse's own loggers.** `handle_new_client_event` logs "Denying new event … User &lt;mxid&gt; not in room …" before raising, and `run_as_background_process` calls `logger.exception` on whatever a background task lets escape. A filter on our loggers cannot touch either. The module's answer to the second is to let **no** exception escape a moderation frame — `_check_and_redact` catches `Exception`, not just `ModerationCheckError`, because the narrower catch made the rule depend on the HTTP client being perfect and a `UnicodeDecodeError` out of `json.loads` was the counterexample: it carried the response body into Synapse's logger. The first is written entirely outside our call stack and cannot be closed from here.
- **An exception's `__context__` is a channel too, and `raise … from None` does not close it.** It clears `__cause__` and stops the traceback being *rendered* with the original; the original stays attached, and a `json.JSONDecodeError` carries the whole response body on `.doc`. And it cannot be fixed by arranging our own frames: the interpreter attaches the active exception at *raise* time, so clearing it in `__init__` is too early, and raising outside our own handler does not help when twisted resumes an awaiting coroutine from inside *its* handler. Shadowing the attribute with a property was worse — it conceals the chain from an ordinary read while `BaseException.__context__.__get__` still returns the original, which is a mask rather than a fix. Each module exception is therefore caught one frame out at the module's boundary, its real slots cleared, and re-raised bare, which does not re-attach.

## Deliberately out of scope here

Teacher/course-admin notification of flagged messages, per-room opt-out, and age-conditional strictness are tracked product gaps in the org doc, not behaviors of this module.
